subject: Using of log predictive density rather than log posterior for measuring predictive accuracy

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Using of log predictive density rather than log posterior for measuring predictive accuracy
parts:
Hi,

I am trying to understand better a section in BDA3:

"Given that we are working with the log predictive density, the question may arise: why not use the log posterior? Why only use the data model and not the prior density in this calculation? The answer is that we are interested here in summarizing the fit of model to data, and for this purpose the prior is relevant for estimating the parameters, but not assessing a model's accuracy."

For some reason, I am finding it hard to understand this. I cannot seem to explain why we don't use the log posterior density for scoring a model. Why wouldn't we want to choose the model that had demonstrated the highest posterior predictive probability of generating a new data point?

Does anyone have any intuitive logic for why this is the case? Or any papers etc. I could read to further explain this? Sorry for my lack of understanding here!

Best,

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using of log predictive density rather than log posterior for measuring predictive accuracy
parts:
The posterior is a distribution over _parameters_ so it doesn’t tell you
anything about prediction.  Prediction is defined by new measurements,
which means you need a distribution over _measurements_.  So
mathematically the posterior isn’t even applicable.

Really the only distribution over measurements that we have are the
distributions defined in the likelihood, but to make a prediction we
need to narrow this down to a single distribution.

In frequentist methods one selects a single “best” parameter and then
uses the corresponding distribution, L(data | theta_best), to make
predictions.  This is especially common in machine learning.

From a Bayesian perspective we can average over the likelihood.
Using the prior gives the prior predictive distribution,

p_{prior predictive} (data_new | data_meas) = \int dtheta L(data_new | theta) p(theta).

This was used by George Box back in the day but has some pathologies
that limits its use.  Instead it’s much more robust to average over
the posterior to incorporate what we’ve learned into the prediction,

p_{post predictive} (data_new | data_meas) = \int dtheta L(data_new | theta) p(theta | data_meas).

This is the formally correct “posterior probability for a new data point”
and is the basis for posterior predictive checks, WAIC, etc.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Using of log predictive density rather than log posterior for measuring predictive accuracy
parts:
Michael's just defining the posterior predictive for you.

The new observations are going to be random variables, just
ones that we happen to observe. This whole data vs. parameter
thing is tricky --- by "data" in Stan we just mean the values
that are observed (constants or modeled data) and by "parameters"
we just mean values we're trying to infer. We try to clarify
these uses in the language section of the manual, following
Gelman and Hill's regression book's classification of variables.

- Bob

Along the same topic, I have some questions related to BDA3.  I have a hard time understanding the log of a "density" as a score because 

1. Density functions are not dimensionless, but have a unit of 1/dy, so it's hard to interpret it.  If the sample contains many iid points, then p(y | theta) = product of p(y_i | theta), which would have a unit of 1/(y^n).

2. A density function could have point values greater than 1 (if it's narrow enough), meaning log(p|theta) can change sign.  That means removing 1 data point away from my y_i's could result in p(y | theta) changing sign.

3. In the broader context of KL divergence, it's hard to picture how the aforementioned sign change would impact the divergence value.  I can imagine situations where D(P || Q) ~ 0 when P and Q are discernibly distant from each other.

Thanks.

Best,

CW

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using of log predictive density rather than log posterior for measuring predictive accuracy
parts: 1. Density functions are not dimensionless, but have a unit of 1/dy, so it's hard to interpret it.  If the sample contains many iid points, then p(y | theta) = product of p(y_i | theta), which would have a unit of 1/(y^n).

Correct — the only well-posed calculation in probability theory are expectations
which reduce to integration.  The dimensionality washes away when you integrate 
a density over some region of parameter space.

2. A density function could have point values greater than 1 (if it's narrow enough), meaning log(p|theta) can change sign.  That means removing 1 data point away from my y_i's could result in p(y | theta) changing sign.

Yes, log p(y | theta) can oscillate between signs as more or less data is considered.
And the exact nature of that oscillation will depend on the parameterization and
hence density that you have chosen.  There’s nothing wrong with that provided
you keep (1) in mind.

3. In the broader context of KL divergence, it's hard to picture how the aforementioned sign change would impact the divergence value.  I can imagine situations where D(P || Q) ~ 0 when P and Q are discernibly distant from each other.

The KL divergence, really any of the divergences from information theory, are
parameterization-invariant — they are maps between probability distributions 
to a number, not densities.  More operationally, all of the odd paramterization-
dependent properties of densities cancels out when you evaluate the 
divergence (or you can write it purely measure-theoretically using 
Radon-Nikodym derivatives, if you’re into that kind of thing).  Really this has
to be true according to (1).

Now all of this gets muddied when people try to argue about quantifying
predictive performance.  The explicit values of the “log predictive density”
score depends on the parameterization, but importantly the _ordering_
of the log predictive density from different models is preserved.  When
the literature discusses log densities as valid “scores” they ultimately are
referring to its ability to determine the ordering between models up to
certain technical assumptions.

Many gory details at https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02273.
